messages.subject: [R-meta] To multivariate (MVMA) or to multi-level meta-analyse (MLMA)
messages.subject_clean: [R-meta] To multivariate (MVMA) or to multi-level meta-analyse (MLMA)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Recently, I have come across several hypertrophy meta-analyses of RCTs
with the following structure:

Study TX–CON SE Location Muscle
A 100 5 Upper Biceps
B 80 4 Upper Triceps
B 90 5 Upper Biceps
C 108 6 Lower RF
C 80 4 Lower VL
D 10 1 Lower VL Type I
D 15 2 Lower VL Type II
D 10 1 Lower VL Type IIb
E 80 4 Trunk Pec

These are typically small meta-analyses. I was introduced to
multilevel meta-analysis (MLMA) through cases such as Study D, where a
study contributes multiple effect sizes to the same comparison (e.g.,
more than two arms).

However, authors are also including different outcomes, such as upper-
versus lower-body muscles, and different muscles within those
anatomical regions. Although these outcomes share an underlying
construct (muscle hypertrophy), they are not necessarily measuring the
same thing.

Given the differences in anatomical location (upper vs. lower body)
and the variation between individual muscles, should these data be
analysed using multilevel (MLMA) or multivariate meta-analysis (MVMA)?

For the purpose of this discussion, I will ignore differences in
assessment methods (CSA vs. muscle thickness vs. muscle volume).



Case II
A real example: https://gyazo.com/eccb4fe57fb9189d291c0929f6628056

Nuñez reports data from seven different anatomical sites.

Would MLMA or MVMA be more appropriate? Is either approach inherently wrong?



Case III

Another example from the same paper:
https://gyazo.com/8da1840567fa5e2d4c5f1d48106769ca

The authors combined countermovement jump (CMJ), drop jump (DJ), and
squat jump (SJ) into a single outcome, "jump performance", which I
think is reasonable when using Hedges' g.

However, Ramírez-Campillo, for example, contributed data from all
three jump tests (CMJ, DJ, and SJ).

The same questions apply: would MLMA or MVMA be more appropriate? Is
either approach inherently wrong?

Thank you!

messages.subject: [R-meta] CHE Model, modified standard errors for funnel  plot, cluster robust tests vs CWB
messages.subject_clean: [R-meta] CHE Model, modified standard errors for funnel  plot, cluster robust tests vs CWB
messages.body_plain:
Dear Mailing list, 

I am conducting a meta-analysis of 28 reports/articles with 30 studies and 110 effect sizes (from POWC and PPWC designs). I would appreciate your advice on three topics.

Topic 1: CHE model and clustering
I account for the fact that ES are nested in studies and sampling errors are correlated (same control group, multiple measurement points, etc.) by using a CHE model with RVE (Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2022). I assume a constant sampling correlation of 0.7 and conduct sensitivity analyses with other values:
V <- vcalc(vi=vi, cluster=Study, obs=ES_ID, rho=0.7, data=dat) 
model <- rma.mv(yi=yi, V=V, random=~1|Study/ES_ID, test = "t?, dfs = "contain?, method="REML", data=dat)
robust(model, cluster=Study, clubSandwich=TRUE)
In almost all cases, a report/article corresponds to a study in my dataset. However, two articles each report two studies based on totally independent samples. For those, I treat the studies as separate clusters. Is this appropriate, or should I account for the shared report by introducing another hierarchical level (report)? Since this concerns only 2 reports, I lean toward my current solution. 

Topic 2: Modified standard errors
Following Chen and Pustejovsky (2026), I'd like to use modified SE for funnel plots and Egger's regression to avoid the artificial association between standardized mean differences and their estimated sampling variances. Here is how I calculate my ES:
# Posttest only with control group designs
POWC <- escalc(measure="SMD", m1i=T_mean, m2i=C_mean, sd1i=T_SD, sd2i=C_SD, n1i=T_N, n2i=C_N, data=POWC)
# Pretest posttest with control group designs
TRE <- escalc(measure="SMCR", m1i=T2_mean, m2i=T1_mean, sd1i=T1_SD, ni=T2_N, ri=corT1T2, data=PPWC)
CON <- escalc(measure="SMCR", m1i=C2_mean, m2i=C1_mean, sd1i=C1_SD, ni=C2_N, ri=corC1C2, data=PPWC)
PPWC$yi <- TRE$yi - CON$yi 
PPWC$vi <- TRE$vi + CON$vi
For POWC designs, does escalc() use the variance formula assumed by Chen and Pustejovsky, such that their proposed modification can be applied directly? For PPWC designs, how should the sampling variances be modified? 

Topic 3: Subgroup analysis and statistical inference
I use an established taxonomy to classify intervention components and examine their effectiveness. For each component, I estimate the pooled effect among interventions containing it and test whether effects differ depending on its presence. Both analyses use the CHE model described above. 
# Model 1: Pooled effects for component absence and presence
model_groups <- rma.mv(yi, V, mods=~current_component-1, random=~1|Study/ES_ID, test = "t?, dfs = "contain?, method="REML", data=dat)
robust(model_groups, cluster=Study, clubSandwich=TRUE)
# Model 2: Difference between component absence and presence
model_difference <-  rma.mv(yi, V, mods=~current_component, random=~1|Study/ES_ID, test = "t?, dfs = "contain?, method="REML", data=dat)
robust(model_difference, cluster=Study, clubSandwich=TRUE)
Many of the cluster robust moderator tests in Model 2 yield low Satterthwaite df (<4). Would you recommend a cluster wild bootstrap for these comparisons (Joshi et al., 2022), and if so, for all components or only those with low df in the cluster robust test (e.g., <2 or <4)? Should CR2 adjustments also be used within CWB? Wald_test_cwb(full_model=model_difference, constraints=constrain_zero(2), R=1999, seed=12345)

I would greatly appreciate any advice or relevant references.


Best regards

Frederk Zirn
PhD student

Literature:
Chen, M., & Pustejovsky, J. E. (2026). Addressing selective reporting bias in meta-analysis of dependent effect sizes: A tutorial in R. Psychological Methods. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000841
Joshi, M., Pustejovsky, J. E., & Beretvas, S. N. (2022). Cluster wild bootstrapping to handle dependent effect sizes in meta-analysis with a small number of studies. Research Synthesis Methods, 13(4), 457?477. https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1554
Pustejovsky, J. E., & Tipton, E. (2022). Meta-analysis with robust variance estimation: Expanding the range of working models. Prevention Science, 23(3), 425?438. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-021-01246-3

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am not entirely sure what distinction you are drawing between a multilevel vs multivariate meta-analysis. Some multivariate models are identical to certain multilevel models, so any comparison would require clearly describing what models are being contrasted.

Best,
Wolfgang

Please see my responses below.

> -----Original Message-----
> From: R-sig-meta-analysis <r-sig-meta-analysis-bounces at r-project.org> On Behalf
> Of Frederik Zirn via R-sig-meta-analysis

> Cc: Frederik Zirn <frederik.zirn at uni-konstanz.de>
> Subject: [R-meta] CHE Model, modified standard errors for funnel plot, cluster
> robust tests vs CWB
> 
> Dear Mailing list,
> 
> I am conducting a meta-analysis of 28 reports/articles with 30 studies and 110
> effect sizes (from POWC and PPWC designs). I would appreciate your advice on
> three topics.
> 
> Topic 1: CHE model and clustering
> I account for the fact that ES are nested in studies and sampling errors are
> correlated (same control group, multiple measurement points, etc.) by using a
> CHE model with RVE (Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2022). I assume a constant sampling
> correlation of 0.7 and conduct sensitivity analyses with other values:
> V <- vcalc(vi=vi, cluster=Study, obs=ES_ID, rho=0.7, data=dat)
> model <- rma.mv(yi=yi, V=V, random=~1|Study/ES_ID, test = "t?, dfs = "contain?,
> method="REML", data=dat)
> robust(model, cluster=Study, clubSandwich=TRUE)
> In almost all cases, a report/article corresponds to a study in my dataset.
> However, two articles each report two studies based on totally independent
> samples. For those, I treat the studies as separate clusters. Is this
> appropriate, or should I account for the shared report by introducing another
> hierarchical level (report)? Since this concerns only 2 reports, I lean toward
> my current solution.

I would also not bother introducing another level here. It would be very difficult to distinguish article level variance from study level variance in this case.
 
> Topic 2: Modified standard errors
> Following Chen and Pustejovsky (2026), I'd like to use modified SE for funnel
> plots and Egger's regression to avoid the artificial association between
> standardized mean differences and their estimated sampling variances. Here is
> how I calculate my ES:
> # Posttest only with control group designs
> POWC <- escalc(measure="SMD", m1i=T_mean, m2i=C_mean, sd1i=T_SD, sd2i=C_SD,
> n1i=T_N, n2i=C_N, data=POWC)
> # Pretest posttest with control group designs
> TRE <- escalc(measure="SMCR", m1i=T2_mean, m2i=T1_mean, sd1i=T1_SD, ni=T2_N,
> ri=corT1T2, data=PPWC)
> CON <- escalc(measure="SMCR", m1i=C2_mean, m2i=C1_mean, sd1i=C1_SD, ni=C2_N,
> ri=corC1C2, data=PPWC)
> PPWC$yi <- TRE$yi - CON$yi
> PPWC$vi <- TRE$vi + CON$vi
> For POWC designs, does escalc() use the variance formula assumed by Chen and
> Pustejovsky, such that their proposed modification can be applied directly? 

No, escalc(measure="SMD", ...) by default uses

vi = 1/n1 + 1/n2 + g^2 / (2*(n1+n2)) 

as the sampling variance (so without the J^2 term). If you want to use equation (4) from that paper, you would neeed to use vtype="LS2". But I would just directly compute the adjusted sampling variance as

vi_mod = 1/n1 + 1/n2

for funnel plots and Egger regression. In essence, we are just leaving out the second term, which is often quite negligible anyway (unless the g value is very large). Say n1=n2=10 and g=0.5. Then 1/10 + 1/10 + 0.5^2 / (2*(10+10)) is 0.20625 while 1/10 + 1/10 is 0.2. So the variance based on the full equation is about 3% larger than when leaving out the second term. So that really makes little difference (but removes the inherent relationship between yi and vi).

> For PPWC designs, how should the sampling variances be modified?

The sampling variance for escalc(measure="SMCR", ...) is computed with

2*(1-r) / n + g^2 / (2*n).

But we have this for each group and then take the sum, so the whole expression for vi is then:

vi = 2*(1-r1) / n1 + g1^2 / (2*n1) + 2*(1-r2) / n2 + g2^2 / (2*n2),

where I use 1 for the first and 2 for the second group in analogy to the POWC case. So leaving out again the term involving the SMCR values themselves, we get:

vi_mod = 2*(1-r1) / n1 + 2*(1-r2) / n2

as the adjusted variance for funnel plots and Egger regression.

> Topic 3: Subgroup analysis and statistical inference
> I use an established taxonomy to classify intervention components and examine
> their effectiveness. For each component, I estimate the pooled effect among
> interventions containing it and test whether effects differ depending on its
> presence. Both analyses use the CHE model described above.
> # Model 1: Pooled effects for component absence and presence
> model_groups <- rma.mv(yi, V, mods=~current_component-1, random=~1|Study/ES_ID,
> test = "t?, dfs = "contain?, method="REML", data=dat)
> robust(model_groups, cluster=Study, clubSandwich=TRUE)
> # Model 2: Difference between component absence and presence
> model_difference <-  rma.mv(yi, V, mods=~current_component,
> random=~1|Study/ES_ID, test = "t?, dfs = "contain?, method="REML", data=dat)
> robust(model_difference, cluster=Study, clubSandwich=TRUE)

Just as a sidenote: You don't actually have to refit the model to get the model 2 results. You can store the robust() results from model 1 and then use anova() / predict() to get the same results. An example:

library(metafor)

dat <- dat.assink2016
V <- vcalc(vi, cluster=study, obs=esid, data=dat, rho=0.6)
res <- rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + deltype, random = ~ 1 | study/esid, data=dat)
rob <- robust(res, cluster=study, clubSandwich=TRUE)
rob

res <- rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ deltype, random = ~ 1 | study/esid, data=dat)
robust(res, cluster=study, clubSandwich=TRUE)

anova(rob, X=rbind(c(-1,1,0), c(-1,0,1)))
predict(rob, newmods=rbind(c(-1,1,0), c(-1,0,1)))

(and when using the robust results only, you can skip test = "t", dfs = "contain"). Nothing wrong with refitting the model, but the whole machinery for testing contrasts and so on is available in metafor.

> Many of the cluster robust moderator tests in Model 2 yield low Satterthwaite df
> (<4). Would you recommend a cluster wild bootstrap for these comparisons (Joshi
> et al., 2022), and if so, for all components or only those with low df in the
> cluster robust test (e.g., <2 or <4)? Should CR2 adjustments also be used within
> CWB? Wald_test_cwb(full_model=model_difference, constraints=constrain_zero(2),
> R=1999, seed=12345)

Using CWB is indeed a useful alternative approach. Whether one uses this by default everywhere or just for cases where the difference may be more noticeable is debatable. Not sure about the CR2 question - that refers to the robust() methods, not? So I don't see how this plays a role with CWB.

> I would greatly appreciate any advice or relevant references.
> 
> Best regards
> Frederk Zirn
> PhD student

> Chen, M., & Pustejovsky, J. E. (2026). Addressing selective reporting bias in
> meta-analysis of dependent effect sizes: A tutorial in R. Psychological Methods.
> https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000841
> Joshi, M., Pustejovsky, J. E., & Beretvas, S. N. (2022). Cluster wild
> bootstrapping to handle dependent effect sizes in meta-analysis with a small
> number of studies. Research Synthesis Methods, 13(4), 457?477.
> https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1554

> estimation: Expanding the range of working models. Prevention Science, 23(3),

Hi Frederik,

Please see below for some further comments, following up on Wolfgang's.

James

On Mon, Nov 9, 2026 at 2:30?AM Frederik Zirn via R-sig-meta-analysis <
r-sig-meta-analysis at r-project.org> wrote:

> Dear Mailing list,
>
> I am conducting a meta-analysis of 28 reports/articles with 30 studies and
> 110 effect sizes (from POWC and PPWC designs). I would appreciate your
> advice on three topics.
>
> Topic 1: CHE model and clustering
> I account for the fact that ES are nested in studies and sampling errors
> are correlated (same control group, multiple measurement points, etc.) by
> using a CHE model with RVE (Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2022). I assume a
> constant sampling correlation of 0.7 and conduct sensitivity analyses with
> other values:
> V <- vcalc(vi=vi, cluster=Study, obs=ES_ID, rho=0.7, data=dat)
> model <- rma.mv(yi=yi, V=V, random=~1|Study/ES_ID, test = "t?, dfs =
> "contain?, method="REML", data=dat)
> robust(model, cluster=Study, clubSandwich=TRUE)
> In almost all cases, a report/article corresponds to a study in my
> dataset. However, two articles each report two studies based on totally
> independent samples. For those, I treat the studies as separate clusters.
> Is this appropriate, or should I account for the shared report by
> introducing another hierarchical level (report)? Since this concerns only 2
> reports, I lean toward my current solution.
>
>
I agree with Wolfgang's response. If you were challenged on treating the
samples as independent, you could do the following:
1. Create the V matrix with cluster = Sample
2. Specify the (working) model with random effects for Sample and ES but
not for study: random = ~ 1 | Sample / ES_ID
3. Cluster the standard errors by study (which works because it is a higher
level factor in which Sample is nested) to account for the possibility of
unmodeled dependence across the samples fin the two studies that have
multiple samples.

This approach would leave your point estimates and variance component
estimates unchanged from your current implementation. Only the standard
errors for average effects / moderator coefficients would change, but I
would guess that the changes will be miniscule (relative to clustering the
standard errors by sample, as in your current implementation).


> Topic 2: Modified standard errors
> Following Chen and Pustejovsky (2026), I'd like to use modified SE for
> funnel plots and Egger's regression to avoid the artificial association
> between standardized mean differences and their estimated sampling
> variances. Here is how I calculate my ES:
> # Posttest only with control group designs
> POWC <- escalc(measure="SMD", m1i=T_mean, m2i=C_mean, sd1i=T_SD,
> sd2i=C_SD, n1i=T_N, n2i=C_N, data=POWC)
> # Pretest posttest with control group designs
> TRE <- escalc(measure="SMCR", m1i=T2_mean, m2i=T1_mean, sd1i=T1_SD,
> ni=T2_N, ri=corT1T2, data=PPWC)
> CON <- escalc(measure="SMCR", m1i=C2_mean, m2i=C1_mean, sd1i=C1_SD,
> ni=C2_N, ri=corC1C2, data=PPWC)
> PPWC$yi <- TRE$yi - CON$yi
> PPWC$vi <- TRE$vi + CON$vi
> For POWC designs, does escalc() use the variance formula assumed by Chen
> and Pustejovsky, such that their proposed modification can be applied
> directly? For PPWC designs, how should the sampling variances be modified?
>
> I agree with Wolfgang. As he noted, the difference between the
conventional SE and the modified SE is very small in most cases, although
it is enough to introduce artifactual correlation between effects and SEs,
thereby biasing Egger's regression test.


> Topic 3: Subgroup analysis and statistical inference
> I use an established taxonomy to classify intervention components and
> examine their effectiveness. For each component, I estimate the pooled
> effect among interventions containing it and test whether effects differ
> depending on its presence. Both analyses use the CHE model described above.
> # Model 1: Pooled effects for component absence and presence
> model_groups <- rma.mv(yi, V, mods=~current_component-1,
> random=~1|Study/ES_ID, test = "t?, dfs = "contain?, method="REML", data=dat)
> robust(model_groups, cluster=Study, clubSandwich=TRUE)
> # Model 2: Difference between component absence and presence
> model_difference <-  rma.mv(yi, V, mods=~current_component,
> random=~1|Study/ES_ID, test = "t?, dfs = "contain?, method="REML", data=dat)
> robust(model_difference, cluster=Study, clubSandwich=TRUE)
> Many of the cluster robust moderator tests in Model 2 yield low
> Satterthwaite df (<4). Would you recommend a cluster wild bootstrap for
> these comparisons (Joshi et al., 2022), and if so, for all components or
> only those with low df in the cluster robust test (e.g., <2 or <4)? Should
> CR2 adjustments also be used within CWB?
> Wald_test_cwb(full_model=model_difference, constraints=constrain_zero(2),
> R=1999, seed=12345)
>
> Joshi's simulations showed that CWB led to improvements in Type I error
and power only for tests with more than 1 *numerator* degree of freedom. If
each of your current_component predictors is a binary variable, then each
test should have just 1 numerator degree of freedom, so I would expect that
you will get very similar results from CWB as you do from just using Wald
tests with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

If some of your predictors have more levels, such that you do have multiple
numerator degrees of freedom, then yes CWB is useful because it both better
controls Type I error and improves power (something that doesn't happen
that often in the world of statistics). If you do need to use CWB, then it
is not necessary to use the CR2 correction as well (it will just slow down
the bootstrap calculations, but is superfluous as far as Type I error
control, per Joshi et al. 2022).

I would greatly appreciate any advice or relevant references.
>
> Best regards
> Frederk Zirn
> PhD student
>
> Literature:
> Chen, M., & Pustejovsky, J. E. (2026). Addressing selective reporting bias
> in meta-analysis of dependent effect sizes: A tutorial in R. Psychological
> Methods. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000841
> Joshi, M., Pustejovsky, J. E., & Beretvas, S. N. (2022). Cluster wild
> bootstrapping to handle dependent effect sizes in meta-analysis with a
> small number of studies. Research Synthesis Methods, 13(4), 457?477.
> https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1554
> Pustejovsky, J. E., & Tipton, E. (2022). Meta-analysis with robust
> variance estimation: Expanding the range of working models. Prevention

messages.body_plain:
Indeed, the term "multivariate" is overloaded, even just within the
meta-analysis literature. I recognize at least three distinct senses (as
described here
https://jepusto.com/posts/what-does-multivariate-mean/index.html).

I suspect that Jorge's question might be using the term to mean a model
with multivariate (correlated) sampling errors, as in the
correlated-and-hierarchical effects model. Beth Tipton and I address the
question of MLMA vs. CHE (or another multivariate working model) in this
paper:
https://jepusto.com/publications/RVE-Meta-analysis-expanding-the-range/
The gist of our argument is that it's beneficial to try and build models
with assumptions that are relatively believable (even if you're ultimately
going to use clustered SEs), recognizing that you're often constrained by
the information available in the primary study reports. In particular, more
plausible working models should give better estimates of heterogeneity,
prediction intervals, and the like.

Following the principle would, I think, point towards using models that
assume some correlation between effect size estimates involving different
measures taken on the same participants, rather than using MLMA, which
assumes zero correlation.

James

R-sig-meta-analysis <r-sig-meta-analysis at r-project.org> wrote:

> Hi,
